blocks: The 70 Weeks (Chathak) & The Cross: The Mathematical Anchor of 1844
How the crucifixion of Christ in A.D. 31 confirms a count that starts in 457 B.C. and reaches 1844.
Big idea

The seventy weeks (490 prophetic years) are severed (chathak) from the 2,300-day timeline, anchoring the entire prophetic calendar in the historical decree of 457 B.C. This reading finds that Jesus Christ arrived and died on the prophetic schedule, in A.D. 31, and it carries the remaining 1,810 years to 1844 on the same line.
In plain words: Daniel 9 gives the seventy weeks as 490 years from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem to the coming of the Messiah, and the cross falls in the middle of the last week.

In Sitting 8, Daniel received the longest time prophecy in the Bible: “Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed” (Daniel 8:14) — the Hebrew nitsdaq means put right. But Gabriel's explanation was cut short: Daniel fainted and was sick certain days, and none understood the vision (Daniel 8:27). The 2,300 days in that chapter have no starting point. Chapter 9 opens years later, in 538 B.C.: the Babylonian empire has fallen to Medo-Persia, Daniel is studying Jeremiah's seventy-year prophecy of the exile, and while he pours out his heart in sackcloth and ashes, Gabriel suddenly reappears to complete the explanation he began at the River Ulai.
Introduction
Daniel's Penitential Prayer and Gabriel's Return
Daniel 9:1–4, 20–23 · Babylon, 538 B.C.

In the first year of Darius the Mede (538 B.C.), Daniel was studying the books of the prophet Jeremiah. He understood by the books that the desolation of Jerusalem would accomplish seventy literal years (Daniel 9:1–2; Jeremiah 25:11–12; 29:10). Since the first deportation occurred in 605 B.C., approximately sixty-seven years had elapsed; the end of the exile was drawing near.

Yet Daniel did not passively wait. Deeply concerned that the sins of his people might prolong their captivity, he set his face toward the Lord God to seek by prayer, supplications, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes (Daniel 9:3). Daniel's intercessory prayer (Daniel 9:4–19) is one of the most sublime confessions in Scripture: though his accusers found no fault in his administration, he confessed his own sin with his people's and repeatedly identified himself with the transgressions of his nation: "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled" (Daniel 9:5).

While Daniel was still speaking in prayer, presenting his supplication for the holy mountain of God, the angel Gabriel—whom he had seen in the vision at the beginning (Daniel 8:16)—flew swiftly and touched him about the time of the evening sacrifice (Daniel 9:20–21). Gabriel announced his divine mission:

"O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding. At the beginning of thy supplications the commandment came forth, and I am come to shew thee; for thou art greatly beloved: therefore understand the matter, and consider the vision." — Daniel 9:22–23 (KJV)

Notice Gabriel's command: "consider the vision." What vision? In Daniel 9, no new symbolic beasts or horns appear. The only vision under discussion is the unexplained 2,300-day vision of Daniel 8, which had caused Daniel to faint and remain sick for days (Daniel 8:27). Gabriel has returned specifically to unlock that very timeline.

Main Point 1
The Hebrew Verb Chathak: Severed from the 2,300 Days
Daniel 9:24
Gabriel immediately begins his explanation by revealing the first portion of the timeline:

"Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy." — Daniel 9:24 (KJV)

A "week" (Hebrew: shabua, שָׁבוּעַ) literally means a unit of seven. Seventy weeks equal 70 × 7, which is 490 prophetic days. Numbers 14:34 and Ezekiel 4:6 appoint each day for a year. In plain words: in this kind of prophecy one day stands for one year of real history. Read that way, the 490 days are 490 literal solar years set apart for Daniel's people and for Jerusalem. Daniel 9:24 names six goals for those weeks: to finish the transgression, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy. On this reading, the first four are met by what Christ does on the cross, where Messiah is cut off for others and the sacrifices stop. The last two fit the sealing, or confirming, of the vision when it is fulfilled, and the anointing of the Most Holy, which this reading ties to Christ's anointing at his baptism. The vision was shut up: in Daniel 8:26 the angel said, "shut thou up the vision; for it shall be for many days." It was shut because the 2,300 days had no starting point. Daniel 9:24 says the weeks are given to "seal up the vision and prophecy", that is, to settle the matter by explaining it. So on this reading the seventy weeks are the answer to the question Daniel was left with: they supply the start the 2,300 days were missing. A reader can check the claim: chapter 8 gives a number and no date, and chapter 9 is where the date is given.
A Word Used Only Once: Chathak Means "Cut"

The English King James Version translates the Hebrew verb as "determined" (Daniel 9:24). However, the inspired word is chathak (חָתַךְ), a word that appears only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament, which scholars call a hapax legomenon.

Later Hebrew and related languages often use chathak for cutting or dividing. Its basic meaning is "properly to cut, to divide ... hence to decree, to determine." Chathak means cut off: the 490 years are cut from the 2,300-year line of Daniel 8:14, joining the two chapters on one start:
Chathak means: "properly to cut, to divide ... hence to decree, to determine."
Rabbinic usage: Chathak is used for cutting off a piece of flesh or trimming a vine.

From what are the seventy weeks (490 years) cut off? They cannot be cut from empty space. They are cut from the only longer time prophecy that Gabriel was sent to explain: the 2,300-day vision of Daniel 8:14. Daniel 8:14 says 2,300 days, and this reading counts them as years by the same day-for-a-year rule it uses for the 490. The lexicon gives "cut" as the root sense of chathak and "decree" or "determine" as a sense that grew from it, and the King James Version chose "determined." This reading keeps the root sense, because Gabriel is explaining a vision whose length is already given, so the weeks are a piece of it. Gabriel states a starting point for the weeks (Daniel 9:25) and none for the 2,300, so this reading takes the 490 years to be the first part of the 2,300. The command in Daniel 9:23 was to consider the vision Daniel had not understood (Daniel 8:27), and a piece cut from the front of that longer span would carry the start the vision was missing. Both then start at the same place in history. The verse does not print that step: it is this reading's inference from Gabriel's command, from the length already given in Daniel 8:14, and from the missing date in Daniel 8.

Main Point 2
Four Persian Decrees: Identifying the 457 B.C. Anchor
Daniel 9:25; Ezra 7:11–26
Gabriel provides the precise historical event that triggers the countdown:

"Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince shall be seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks: the street shall be built again, and the wall, even in troublous times." — Daniel 9:25 (KJV)

Persian monarchs issued several royal commissions regarding the Jewish return. Bible students often compare three restoring decrees (Cyrus, Darius, Artaxerxes). This sitting adds Nehemiah’s wall commission as a fourth line on the chart — a permit under Artaxerxes, not a new charter for Daniel 9:25:
Persian commissions compared (three decrees + Nehemiah permit)

1. The Decree of Cyrus the Great (538/537 B.C. · Ezra 1:1–4): Cyrus authorized the exiles to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. It contained no authorization to restore municipal self-government, appoint judges, or rebuild the civil city.

2. The Decree of Darius I Hystaspes (520 B.C. · Ezra 6:1–12): When Samaritan adversaries halted temple construction, Darius confirmed Cyrus's original edict. This was purely a reaffirmation of temple rebuilding, adding no civil or administrative authority.

3. The Decree of Artaxerxes I Longimanus (Autumn 457 B.C. · Ezra 7:11–26): In the seventh year of his reign, Artaxerxes sent Ezra the scribe a royal order, called a firman. It gave Ezra full civil authority: to appoint magistrates and judges, to teach and enforce the laws of God and the king, and to punish by death, banishment, confiscation of goods, or imprisonment (Ezra 7:25–26). This reading takes it to be the only decree that both restored the Jews' own government and led to the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem. The sign that building went on under it is Ezra 4:12, where officials complain that the Jews who came up from Artaxerxes are "building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof."

4. The Commission to Nehemiah (444 B.C. · Nehemiah 2:1–8): In his twentieth year, Artaxerxes granted Nehemiah personal permission and timber to rebuild the physical walls of Jerusalem. This was a permit to finish the walls under the existing 457 B.C. decree. It gave Nehemiah timber and royal backing, but it did not give the Jews a new government, because the 457 B.C. decree had already done that.

Here is why this reading starts the count with the third line on that chart and not the first two. Daniel 9:25 asks for a command "to restore and to build Jerusalem", the city and not the temple only. Cyrus and Darius gave orders about the temple, and the Nehemiah permit of 444 B.C. only let walls be finished under a decree already given. The seventh-year order to Ezra gave judges, laws, and punishments, which are the powers of a working city government, and the building that followed it is what the officials complained about in Ezra 4:12. That is why the count starts here. By the Jewish civil calendar, which began each year in the autumn, the seventh year of Artaxerxes I Longimanus ran from autumn 458 B.C. to autumn 457 B.C. Ezra 7:8 says Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month of that seventh year, so he arrived in the summer of 457 B.C. This reading counts both the 70-week line and the 2,300-year line from the autumn of 457 B.C., the first autumn after the decree took effect.
Main Point 3
The 69 Weeks to Messiah: The Anointing in A.D. 27
Daniel 9:25 subdivides the 70 weeks into distinct chronological segments: "seven weeks, and threescore and two weeks" (69 weeks) until Messiah the Prince:
Seven weeks equal 49 prophetic days, which are 49 solar years (the time to clear the debris and rebuild Jerusalem's streets and walls in "troublous times").
Sixty-two weeks equal 434 prophetic days, which are 434 solar years.
Total: 69 weeks equal 7 + 62, which is 483 prophetic days, or 483 literal solar years.
The Mathematical Walk: 457 B.C. to A.D. 27 (Accounting for No Year Zero)

In historical and astronomical chronology, there is no year zero between B.C. and A.D. The timeline moves immediately from December 31, 1 B.C. to January 1, A.D. 1. Therefore, when walking across the B.C./A.D. divide, one year must be added, to delete the nonexistent zero year:

Here is the same walk in words, so you can do it yourself. Start at autumn 457 B.C., the autumn the decree took effect. Count forward 483 whole years. That count crosses the line between the years before Christ and the years after him, and because no year zero sits on that line, one year is added back: 483 years counted from 457 B.C. reach 26, and 26 plus the missing year is 27. So the count lands in Autumn A.D. 27. It lands in the autumn because a whole number of years counted from an autumn ends in an autumn, and this reading starts the count in the autumn of 457 B.C.

What occurred in Autumn A.D. 27? Luke 3:1 dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar." Tiberius became emperor in A.D. 14. Counting years from autumn to autumn, as the Jews did, his first year ended in the autumn of A.D. 14, so his fifteenth year began in the autumn of A.D. 27. Soon after, Jesus of Nazareth came to the Jordan River to be baptized by John (Luke 3:21–23). As He went up straightway out of the water (Matthew 3:16), the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the bodily form of a dove (Luke 3:22), and the Father's voice proclaimed: "Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased."

The Hebrew word Mashiach (Messiah) and the Greek word Christos both mean "the Anointed One." Luke 2:11 calls him Christ at his birth. He was anointed for his public mission by the Holy Spirit at His baptism in A.D. 27 (Acts 10:38). Daniel 9:25 speaks of the Messiah as he appears to begin his work, so the anointing at the baptism, not the birth, is the date that matches. After forty days in the wilderness (Mark 1:12–13) and after John was imprisoned (Mark 1:14), Jesus entered Galilee preaching the gospel of the kingdom and proclaiming:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." — Mark 1:15 (KJV)
What "time" was fulfilled? Mark does not name Daniel, but this reading hears in Jesus' words the end of the 69 weeks of Daniel 9:25, the time set for the arrival of Messiah the Prince.

49 years (7 weeks) to 408 B.C.

Ezra 7 records the seventh year of Artaxerxes I, and this sitting reads it as 457 B.C. It is the decree that gives Jerusalem its own government again, which is what Daniel 9:25 asks for when it speaks of a command to restore and to build Jerusalem. The four decrees are compared in the table above: only this one restores city and state.
The seven weeks end
Troublous times. 434 years (62 weeks) to A.D. 27.

The first seven weeks (49 years) cover the rebuilding of the city, and Daniel 9:25 says it happens in troublous times. This sitting reaches 408 B.C. by counting, not from a record. The sixty-two weeks then run 434 years from 408 B.C. to A.D. 27; the two spans are consecutive, not overlapping.
Baptism of Jesus
Anointed at the Jordan. 69 weeks complete.

Luke dates the baptism in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and has Jesus praying as the heaven opens and the Spirit descends on him. Sixty-nine of the seventy weeks land here, which is the checkpoint the reckoning rests on: a dated decree at one end, a dated baptism at the other.

Main Point 4
The Midst of the Week: The Cross in A.D. 31 and Sacrifices Ceasing
Daniel 9:26–27; Matthew 27:50–51; Hebrews 9:26; 10:12

With 69 weeks completed in Autumn A.D. 27, exactly one prophetic week (7 literal years) remained of the 70-week covenant allotment. Daniel 9:26–27 records what transpires in this momentous final week:

"And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself... And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease..." — Daniel 9:26–27 (KJV)
1. Messiah Cut Off: He Died in Our Place

Daniel 9:26 declares that Messiah would be "cut off, but not for himself." To be cut off is to be put to death, cut off from the living. The Hebrew phrase ve'en lo means that He was not cut off for a crime of His own; there was no guilt of his own for him to die for. That is the reason the death was for others: if it was not for his own sin, then he was bearing the sin of someone else. He died as an innocent substitute for the sins of the world. Isaiah 53:5 foretold the same reality: "He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities."
2. The Midst of the Week: Spring A.D. 31

The final week of seven years ran from Autumn A.D. 27 to Autumn A.D. 34. The middle of a seven-year week is three and a half years in, so three and a half years after Autumn A.D. 27 lands in Spring A.D. 31. In Spring A.D. 31, at the feast of the Passover, Jesus Christ was crucified on Calvary. That date follows from counting to the “midst of the week” in Daniel 9:27, so it comes from the count itself. The Gospels fit it: John mentions Passovers during Jesus' ministry (John 2:13; 6:4; 13:1), which suits a ministry of about three and a half years from his baptism to the last Passover.
3. Causing Sacrifices to Cease: The Rent Veil

At the exact moment Jesus died on the cross crying "It is finished" (John 19:30), "the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom" (Matthew 27:51). The veil hung in the temple between the holy place and the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest could go. Its tearing from top to bottom shows that the way to God was now open through Christ. The earthly sacrifices were a type, a picture pointing ahead to his death, and the cross is the antitype, the real thing the picture pointed to. By offering His own precious blood once for all, Jesus brought a permanent end to the divine necessity and efficacy of earthly animal sacrifices (Hebrews 9:11–12; 10:1–14). No ruler issued an order in that hour to stop the temple sacrifices; the veil tore as he died, and this reading takes that tearing as the sign that their work was finished.
4. The Close of the 70 Weeks: Autumn A.D. 34

The remaining 3.5 years of the 70th week ran from Spring A.D. 31 to Autumn A.D. 34. During this period, the disciples bore witness in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth (Acts 1:8; Acts 8). Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:54–60). Autumn A.D. 34 closes the seventieth week, three and a half years after the cross, as the gospel turns to the wider Gentile mission after Stephen (Acts 7–8). The stoning of Stephen closes the seventy weeks allotted to Daniel's people and city (9:24). After Stephen's death, the believers were scattered and bore witness beyond Jerusalem (Acts 8:1–4); Saul of Tarsus was converted on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–9). The year A.D. 34 is an inference from the half-week and from Acts, not a year the text prints. In plain words: the seventieth week is the last seven years of the 490, running from the baptism in A.D. 27 to the autumn of A.D. 34, with the cross at its middle. So the seventy weeks are not still waiting to be fulfilled; on this reading they finished in the first century, among Daniel's own people and city. For a reader today that means the covenant blessings of the week are already open: the gospel has gone out to the nations, and no future seven-year countdown has to start before the prophecy can come true.

Main Point 5
Refuting the Dispensationalist Gap: Christ Confirms the Covenant
Why the 70th week belongs to Jesus, not a future Antichrist

In the nineteenth century, John Nelson Darby, and later the Scofield Reference Bible, spread a form of futurism called dispensationalism. It says the 70th week was cut off from the other 69 and put on hold for more than two thousand years. It then expects that week to run in the future as seven years of great trouble under one individual antichrist. People hold this view because they expect a final crisis before Christ returns, and they look for a place to put it in Daniel. Its best case is that verse 27 has its own covenant and its own end of sacrifice, and a gap lets those details land in a still-future crisis instead of at the cross. A second rival reading goes the other way and puts the whole prophecy in the past: it ends the weeks with the Greek ruler Antiochus, whose persecution is described outside this chapter, and with the cleansing of the temple altar in 164 B.C. People hold that reading because the last week's details, an anointed one cut off, sacrifice stopping, and a desolator, sound like that persecution, and because it keeps the prophecy inside the Old Testament period. This course answers that Daniel 9:25 runs the weeks "unto the Messiah the Prince", and 483 years from the decree land in the first century, not the second century B.C.; the sacrifices cease here because the true sacrifice has come, not because a foreign king defiled an altar. But Daniel 9 does not give the gap its place either. There are four reasons:
Four reasons the gap does not fit Daniel 9

1. Who is "he"? From verse 25 to verse 27 the angel is speaking about one person: "Messiah the Prince" in verse 25, "Messiah" cut off in verse 26, and then "he" in verse 27: "And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week." The only other figure in verse 26 is "the people of the prince that shall come," and it is those people who destroy the city, not the prince. So "he" is the Messiah the angel has been following all along, and not a future antichrist. A reader might take "he" to be the Roman general Titus, because his troops destroyed the city and the sanctuary in A.D. 70 and verse 26 names that destruction just before the word "he." This reading says the destroyers are called the people of the prince, not the prince himself, and the angel has already named Messiah twice, so "he" is the Messiah.

2. Which covenant is confirmed? The word "antichrist" appears only in John's letters (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7), and none of those verses speaks of him making a covenant. In the Bible, "the covenant" is God's covenant with his people, and Jesus is the one who confirmed it. The prophets promised a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34), and Hebrews 8:8–13 shows Christ bringing it. That is the covenant this reading sees in Daniel 9:27. At the Last Supper, Jesus held the cup and said: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28; Hebrews 8:8–13). "Testament" here means covenant, that is, the agreement between God and his people. To confirm a covenant is to make it firm, to carry it out so that it stands. Christ confirmed that covenant through his life and his death.

3. No verse prints the gap. Nothing in the text says that the clock stops between the 69th and 70th weeks. The seventy weeks are given as one block of 490 years that is "determined," or cut off (chathak), as a single unit. The gap view takes the 70th week, with its covenant and its end of sacrifices, away from Jesus and gives them to a future ruler, who is said to make a treaty and then break it. In this reading the one who confirms the covenant and causes the sacrifice and the oblation to cease is Jesus himself, and he does it in the middle of the week by dying. That is the work of Christ on the cross.

4. Why the count carries on to 1844: Since 490 years of the 2,300-year line were completed in A.D. 34, 1,810 years remained (2,300 − 490). Measuring 1,810 years from autumn A.D. 34 brings us directly to autumn 1844 (34 + 1,810 = 1844). The same count has now fit two events in the Gospels, the baptism in A.D. 27 and the cross in A.D. 31, so this reading trusts the same count for the rest of the line. The 1844 end is carried by the count, not by a separate record.

INTERPRETATION

Daniel 9 answers the question Daniel 8 left hanging. Chapter 8 gave a span of 2,300 days and no starting point, and Daniel says plainly that he did not understand it (Daniel 8:27). Chapter 9 supplies the start, and it supplies it in the middle of a prayer about something else.

Gabriel comes back and tells Daniel to consider the vision (Daniel 9:23), then gives him seventy weeks. Those weeks are 70 times 7, which is 490 days. Read as literal days they come to about sixteen months, far too short to rebuild a city, restore a nation, and see the Messiah arrive and die. Read on the year-day scale the Bible itself supplies, they are 490 years, and they run from the decree to restore Jerusalem to the coming of the Messiah.

Three things follow, and this sitting walks each one. First, the weeks have a starting point in history: the decree that actually authorized rebuilding the city, which this reading takes to be the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7), in 457 B.C. Second, they have a shape: seven weeks, then sixty-two weeks, then one week, with the Messiah cut off in the middle of that last week. Third, they have an end, in A.D. 34, when the seventy weeks close.

Notice what the arithmetic is doing. The dates are not the point. The cross is the point, and the dates are what make the cross the center of the count. The one who arranged the return from exile, the rebuilding of the city, and the arrival of the Messiah is the same God who told Daniel the number in advance.

The bottom line is what the seventieth week is and where it ends. It is not a week still waiting in our future, separated from the other sixty-nine by a gap no verse prints. It is the week of the Messiah's own ministry, and its middle is the cross. Everything this sitting adds, including the reasons the other readings do not fit, is in service of that one claim.
CHRIST

Jesus Christ is the divine Center of Daniel 9. He was anointed at the Jordan in A.D. 27, cut off for our sins at Calvary in A.D. 31, and confirmed the everlasting covenant with His own blood. The cross falls in the middle of the last of the seventy weeks, so the count has now fit both the baptism and the cross. This reading therefore carries the same count forward. The 1,810 years still left after A.D. 34 end in 1844. Heavenly sanctuary ministry means Christ's work in heaven as high priest, the cleansing Daniel 8:14 named, which this reading places at the end of that count.
Practical Application
Resting on the Dated Rock of Calvary
Daniel 9 provides profound assurance for every believer walking in a secularized world:
1. Trust God's sovereign control over human history

God orchestrated the decrees of Persian emperors and Messiah's crucifixion centuries in advance. The God who manages global history with mathematical precision is fully capable of managing every detail of your personal life. Here is the practice: this week, when a headline frightens you, write the headline down, and beside it write one dated line from this sitting, the decree of 457 B.C. or the cross in A.D. 31; then thank God that he keeps his word on time.
2. Confess sin for others, the way Daniel did

Daniel's prayer in sackcloth and ashes shows that true revival begins with personal and corporate confession. When the church faces spiritual decline, the answer is not political agitation but falling on our faces before God, acknowledging our sins, and pleading for His covenant mercy. Here is the practice: in your next prayer, name one sin of your own family or church and say "we" rather than "they," the way Daniel prayed.
3. Cling to the completed atonement of the Cross

Messiah was cut off, but not for Himself. He bore your guilt, your shame, and your death penalty on Calvary. Earthly sacrifices have ceased because Christ's blood is all-sufficient. You do not need earthly priests or human penance; rest entirely in the finished sacrifice of Jesus. Here is the practice: today, name one wrong you keep trying to pay for yourself, say it to God in plain words, and thank him that the payment is already made.
4. Stand firm on the prophetic chain

Do not be tossed about by speculative theories that insert a future seven-year gap. On this reading the cross fell in A.D. 31 and the sanctuary cleansing began in 1844, each on the line the count gives. Here is the practice: when someone hands you a prophecy chart, find the cross on it first, and ask who confirms the covenant in Daniel 9:27. God's prophetic word is sure, steadfast, and unshakeable.
The principle to remember
TEXT — Does Daniel 9:24 use the verb chathak ("cut off") to sever 490 years from the 2,300 days?
HISTORY — Did Artaxerxes' decree in 457 B.C. uniquely restore civil governance and magistrates to Jerusalem?
INTERPRETATION — Does the count, allowing for no year zero, land on the baptism in A.D. 27 and the cross in A.D. 31?
CHRIST — Did Jesus confirm the New Covenant in His blood in the midst of the week, ending earthly animal sacrifices?
Messiah Cut Off: The Mathematical Anchor of Prophecy

In Daniel 9, the focal point of the entire prophetic calendar converges upon the Person and work of Jesus Christ. Gabriel announces that sixty-nine prophetic weeks (483 literal years) from the Persian decree in 457 B.C. would reach 'unto the Messiah the Prince' (Daniel 9:25). In Autumn A.D. 27, precisely on schedule, Jesus was anointed by the Holy Spirit at His baptism in the Jordan (Luke 3:21–22). After the wilderness and after John was imprisoned, he preached in Galilee: 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand' (Mark 1:15).

In the midst of the seventieth week—Spring A.D. 31—the divine climax occurred: Messiah was 'cut off, but not for himself' (Daniel 9:26). On Calvary's cross, Jesus bore our sins in His own body. In that awful, sacred hour, the temple veil tore from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51), signifying that the picture had met the real thing it pointed to, that earthly animal sacrifices had ceased to possess divine efficacy, and Christ had confirmed the everlasting covenant through His own shed blood.

Rejoice in the immovable historical certainty of your salvation. Because the count lands on the baptism in A.D. 27 and on the cross in A.D. 31, this reading carries the same count along the rest of the line, and the remaining 1,810 years reach 1844. Stand secure in the righteousness of the One who was cut off for you, knowing that your High Priest now intercedes in the heavenly sanctuary until His kingdom is fully revealed.
